examples.question_text:
The table shows the masses of parcels.

| Mass $m$ (kg) | Frequency $f$ |
|---|---:|
| $0<m\le2$ | 4 |
| $2<m\le6$ | 8 |
| $6<m\le12$ | 6 |
| $12<m\le20$ | 2 |

Estimate the mean mass, correct to 2 decimal places.
examples.solution_text:
Each class centre is the average of its two endpoints. For the first class, $cc=\dfrac{0+2}{2}=1$.

| Mass $m$ (kg) | $f$ | $cc$ | $cc\times f$ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| $0<m\le2$ | 4 | 1 | 4 |
| $2<m\le6$ | 8 | 4 | 32 |
| $6<m\le12$ | 6 | 9 | 54 |
| $12<m\le20$ | 2 | 16 | 32 |
| Total | 20 | | 122 |

$\begin{align*}\overline{x}&=\frac{\Sigma(cc\times f)}{\Sigma f}\\&=\frac{122}{20}\\&=6.10\text{ kg}\end{align*}$

examples.question_text:
The table shows the ages of visitors to a museum.

| Age $a$ (years) | Frequency |
|---|---:|
| $0<a\le20$ | 6 |
| $20<a\le40$ | 10 |
| $40<a\le60$ | 9 |
| $60<a\le80$ | 6 |

(a) State the modal class and find the median class.

(b) One more visitor, aged 70, joins the group. Find the median class for the resulting 32 visitors.

(c) A separate group has frequencies 6, 10, 10 and 6 in the same four classes. Explain whether its median class can be determined uniquely.
examples.solution_text:
(a) The highest frequency is 10, so the modal class is $20<a\le40$.

$\begin{align*}n&=6+10+9+6\\&=31\\\text{Median position}&=\frac{31+1}{2}\\&=16\end{align*}$

The cumulative frequencies are 6, 16, 25 and 31. The 16th visitor lies in $20<a\le40$, so this is the median class.

(b) The cumulative frequencies become 6, 16, 25 and 32. The middle observations are at positions 16 and 17. They lie in $20<a\le40$ and $40<a\le60$, respectively. Their exact ages are unknown, so their average could lie in either class. A unique median class cannot be determined.

(c) The cumulative frequencies are 6, 16, 26 and 32. Again, positions 16 and 17 lie in different classes. A unique median class cannot be determined from the grouped table.

examples.question_text:
Five travel times are $12,13,14,15,16$ minutes. They are grouped into the single class $10<t\le20$.

(a) Calculate the exact mean and the grouped mean estimate.

(b) Explain why the grouped mean is an estimate and why it is higher in this case.
examples.solution_text:
(a) $\begin{align*}\text{Exact mean}&=\frac{12+13+14+15+16}{5}\\&=\frac{70}{5}\\&=14\text{ min}\end{align*}$

$\begin{align*}cc&=\frac{10+20}{2}\\&=15\\\text{Grouped mean estimate}&=\frac{15\times5}{5}\\&=15\text{ min}\end{align*}$

(b) Grouping loses the individual values. The calculation replaces each value with the class centre, 15 minutes. The actual mean is 14 minutes, so the estimate is 1 minute higher. A grouped estimate can be higher, lower or equal to the exact mean.

examples.question_text:
The table shows the ages of concert attendees.

| Age $a$ (years) | Frequency |
|---|---:|
| $16<a\le30$ | 12 |
| $30<a\le45$ | 18 |
| $45<a\le65$ | 14 |
| $65<a$ | 6 |

Explain why the class-centre method cannot give an estimated mean age from this table.
examples.solution_text: The class $65<a$ has no upper endpoint, so its class centre cannot be calculated. The class-centre method needs a centre for every class with a nonzero frequency.

coverage.summary: Authored five worked examples covering all six distinct assessed methods with changed values and separate question and solution fields. The ogive includes solution-only median guides. Prose remains editable and inherits blue solution styling. All 25 retained assessments were classified only; their mathematics was neither altered nor re-audited. No files were written. Independent review and actual visual verification remain for the coordinator.

examples.derivation: Class centres are 1, 4, 9 and 16. Weighted products are 4, 32, 54 and 32, totalling 122. Total frequency is 20, so the estimated mean is 122/20 = 6.10 kg. Unequal class widths do not change the taught class-centre method.

Initially n = 31 and cumulative frequencies are 6, 16, 25, 31. The modal class and the class containing observation 16 are both 20 < a ≤ 40. Adding the visitor gives cumulative frequencies 6, 16, 25, 32; middle observations 16 and 17 occupy different classes. Their average can fall in either class. The separate group has cumulative frequencies 6, 16, 26, 32 and the same ambiguity.

The final cumulative frequency is 60, so the 50% line is 30. The segment from (20,18) to (30,42) crosses cumulative frequency 30 halfway between its endpoints, at 25 minutes. Solution-only guides correctly follow (0,30) to (25,30) to (25,0). Question and solution curves match; the question contains no answer guides.

The observations total 70, giving an exact mean of 14 minutes. The class centre is (10+20)/2 = 15, giving a grouped estimate of (15×5)/5 = 15 minutes. The estimate exceeds the exact mean by 1 minute because the class-centre replacement increases the total from 70 to 75.
The final class 65 < a contains six attendees but has no upper endpoint. Its class centre and weighted contribution cannot be determined, preventing the specified class-centre mean calculation.

review.summary: All six distinct assessed methods are mapped and covered by the five examples. All 25 exact assessment locators are present; accepted assessment mathematics was not re-audited. The supplied source supports the methods, with the even-sample clarification retained from accepted theory. There are no existing examples to audit. Separate editable prompts and solutions, equation gutters, diagram coordinates and solution-only annotations are sound. Blue prose and mathematics rely on the confirmed renderer. Final rendered typography and layout verification remain for the coordinator.
